Turns cost into a plan.
The measured cost per run from neatlogs goes into the pricing model. ### neatlogs Shows What the Agent Did Each run is one `firstrun.run` trace. The span kinds are WORKFLOW, AGENT, TOOL and GUARDRAIL. Claude calls appear as typed LLM spans.

One trace per run. Reading, planning, every step and verification sit under one root span.
A custom detection. "Docs step broke" flags failed tool spans. 40 flagged.

Detection analysis. 132 traces, 154 errors. "Docs step broke" hit 35 times, 12.9%.
Investigate. A 52.8x spike in Execution Failed opened a root cause with a confidence score.

Recovery spans. Classify, search, patch and retry show as `recover.N` spans.
Analytics. 132 traces and $0.9071 total cost, in one view.
Two detections run on the traces: "docs step broke" and "planner invented a step". The second one flagged 3 planner spans in v1. Investigate traced them to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one ([evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md](evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md)). A Claude Code session read the detection and its trend over the neatlogs MCP server and applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11. The fix adds code guards that drop invented, placeholder and fake-secret steps. The integration check read 3 real runs back from persisted traces. See [docs/neatlogs-integration.md](docs/neatlogs-integration.md). ### Entire Records How the Build Happened

A checkpoint on each agent commit. The commit maps back to the session that wrote it.
A merge gate. The merge stays blocked while a high finding is open.
Inline review. The finding sits on the line in src/firstrun/recovery.py.
- **Checkpoints:** 91 of 132 non-merge commits on main up to `f5d73eb` carry an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer, counted with `git log --no-merges` on 2026-10-11. The 41 without are the 4 setup commits before the first agent session and site commits from 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-11. On many of those the Entire commit hook hung and was stopped so the commit could land. Merge commits carry none, because Entire's hook skips merges. The neatlogs fix commit shows the full agent session behind it: [checkpoint 01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/3ca6f118ecb0a8915315eea27b5588dd8a7c6299). - **Trail reviews:** Entire runners reviewed every layer on Trails 3 to 7. They raised 2 real bugs on Layer 1, a secret retry loop and a Windows-only Docker default, both fixed in e2aacb7. - **Trails:** [Trail 1](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/trails/1) covers Layer 1. Trail pages need an entire.io login. The commit and session pages open without one. - **Graph:** the build agents searched the repo through the graph. 4 graph calls saved about 11,662 tokens. - **Brain:** it holds 7 durable facts, such as why recovery stops at 3 attempts. Its last refresh indexed 63 files and 1,056 symbols. ### cfo.ai Prices the Nightly Check

Ari, the cfo.ai agent, on day one.		 The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads 88 neatlogs traces and writes [business/drivers.csv](business/drivers.csv) for cfo.ai. The mean run costs $0.0178, and the p95 run costs $0.0529. A 70% margin floor turns those costs into a cap per tier, and `firstrun run --tier scale` stops any run that spends past the cap. | Tier | Price | Quickstarts | Cap per run | Runs over the cap | |---|---|---|---|---| | Free | $0 | 1, weekly | $0.0135 | 50.0% | | Team | $49 a month | 10, nightly | $0.0470 | 9.1% | | Scale | $299 a month | 100, nightly, with PRs, Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | $0.0279 | 26.1% | The old fixed cap of $0.50 let one bad month cost a Scale customer's fee five times over. The plan, the Scale fix and every assumption are in [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md). The cfo.ai model is public at [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE). Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. The [plan page](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/plan/) shows the caps, the measured cost spread and the cash per Scenario. Every doc-test run is tagged against the caps. A neatlogs alert uses the Scale cap as its threshold, and `scripts/neatlogs_issues.py` mirrors each detection and alert as a GitHub issue labeled [`neatlogs`](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/issues?q=label%3Aneatlogs).
### Every Run and Audit Ends With a Receipt A receipt turns one unit of agent work into a priced, capped, verified and checkable record. [A sample bill](docs/receipts/FR-20261010-091740-help-accuknox-com.html) for the AccuKnox knoxctl run shows the parts: ----- ``` FirstRun ran this section on itself in a clean `python:3.11-slim` container. The install failed until git was present, which is why git is listed above. The run step then stopped with the missing-token message, because a clean container has no Claude token or Docker. ## One Trace Follows the Docs Page From Read to Verified Fix ```mermaid flowchart TD A[docs URL] --> B["read_docs
Firecrawl · TOOL"] B --> C["planner
Claude Sonnet 5.5 · AGENT"] C --> D[runbook.json] D --> E["step.N in a fresh container
TOOL"] E --> F{step failed?} F -- no, next step --> E F -- no, last step --> I F -- yes --> G["classify_failure
Jev, ask once below 0.7, precedents.json · TOOL"] G --> H["recover.N
search, patch, max 3 attempts · AGENT"] H --> E H -- gave up --> J[report.md, failed] I["verify
new container, no model calls · GUARDRAIL"] --> K["report.md
patch.diff
pr_body.md"] ``` A `budget` GUARDRAIL span runs before every recovery. The root span `firstrun.run` is a WORKFLOW span that holds the whole tree. [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) lists the states, the failure classes, the budgets and every span. ## Each of the 8 Focus Areas Has a Feature You Can Open | Focus area | Feature | Where you see it | |---|---|---| | Planning | The planner turns the docs page into a runbook | `runbook.json`, the `planner` span | | Tool use | Firecrawl reads, Docker runs, Jev classifies | One TOOL span per call | | State | `state.json` is written after every step | `firstrun run --resume RUN_ID` | | Context | The planner reads only the quickstart page | `read_docs` span input | | Execution | One fresh container per run | `step.N` spans with exit codes | | Recovery | Classify, search, patch, retry up to 3 times | `recover.N` span | | Verification | A model-free re-run in a new container | `verify` span, status `verified` | | Iteration | v1 traces, detections, a fix, v2 traces | The results table below | ## Version 2 Finishes 3 of 4 Quickstarts and Recovers 3 Failed Steps v1 ran with recovery off. v2 ran after the neatlogs planner fix (3ca6f11), with recovery and verification on. The same four targets ran both times. Cost and duration come from the neatlogs traces in [evidence/before_after_traces.json](evidence/before_after_traces.json). Cost is the Sonnet 5.5 list price and is not billed, because the runs use a subscription token. | Target | v1 (recovery off) | v2 (neatlogs fix, recovery, verify) | |---|---|---| | neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 | passed 3/3 | | Entire CLI install | failed at step 1, `curl: command not found` | verified 4/4 after 2 fixes, one of them a real docs fix | | Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 | passed 2/2 | | OpenAI v0 README (fixture, Wayback 2023-08-02) | failed at step 6, `openai: command not found` | pinned `openai==0.28.1`, then stopped honestly: the example needs an OpenAI key | | Metric | v1 | v2 | |---|---|---| | Quickstarts that end passed or verified | 2 of 4 | 3 of 4 | | Failed steps recovered | 0 | 3 | | Fixes proven in a fresh container | 0 | 1 | | Average tool spans per run | 4.25 | 6.0 | | Average cost per run, from neatlogs | $0.0262 | $0.0200 | | Average run time, verification included | 128 s | 201 s | v2 takes longer because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart a second time in a new container. The six mistakes the agent made in v1: 1. The plan changes between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later. 2. The planner invents steps. It added `command -v entire` and `test -f first_trace.py`, which the docs never say. 3. The planner writes placeholder steps. Chroma step 2 is `true`. 4. A fake secret passes as a step. `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0. 5. The planner skips the steps that matter, because they need a key. 6. 9 of 16 steps check only the exit code. ## What Broke While Building - **Git 2.33 hung Entire checkpoints.** The post-commit hook waited 206 s on `git update-ref --stdin`, and the checkpoint was never written. Git 2.55.0 fixed it, and the next hook took 3 s. - **One run split into 3 traces.** The first live run on the neatlogs docs produced 3 traces. The CLI now opens one `firstrun.run` trace around reading, planning, every step and verification. - **Ask-once crashed background runs.** The prompt raised `EOFError` with no terminal. It now returns nothing, and recovery uses the top class. - **Tests exported junk traces.** Each `pytest` run created about 50 empty `neatlogs-app` traces. The test fixture now sets an empty key, and a run after the fix created 0 traces. - **A docs note looked like a docs bug.** On Dagster, FirstRun labeled two gaps as docs bugs. A check of the source showed the page already covers both, in a prerequisite line and a note the planner skipped. FirstRun now opens no PR on Dagster. Every PR draft gets a source check before it ships. - **A cd broke steps three ways.** A leading cd, a cd inside a patched chain, and a file check after cd each failed a step that worked. The container now treats a cd into the folder it is already in as a no-op, and file checks also look from the run root. - **The Entire Brain watcher does not run on Windows.** Brain runs with `--no-daemon` and is refreshed by hand. Known limits are listed in [docs/known-limits.md](docs/known-limits.md). Examples: a hung step is not retried, and version pinning covers pip only. ## Parallel Agents Built It and Entire Reviewed Every Layer - **Build:** a lead session planned the work and ran worker agents in parallel, one track each: fixtures, planner, executor, recovery, verification, report page, then edge cases. All agents ran on Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort. - **Review:** each layer is an Entire Trail, so Entire runners reviewed every commit since kickoff. They found 3 real bugs, all fixed: a secret retry loop, a Windows-only Docker default, and a cd guard that was written but never called. - **CI:** GitHub Actions runs the offline suite on every push and pull request. On the launch branch on 2026-10-11 the offline suite gave 384 passed, 68 skipped (they need `FIRSTRUN_LIVE=1` or a human check) and 1 expected failure. - **Jury self-test:** the Entire judge plugin, run on this repo with the real start time, ranked it with no excluded work: 3.93 of 5, authenticity 4.5, integrity 5.0. The report is [evidence/jury-selftest.txt](evidence/jury-selftest.txt). Planning happened before the event in a private repo. The build log is [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).

> **Purpose:** This is the top rule for any writing that another person will read. Every other
> writing file sits under it. [Voice](./Voice.md) says how it sounds. [Long-Form Writing
> Rules](./Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) says how it is built. `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`
> says what is banned. This file says what the writing is for.
>
> Adapted from Clay's internal AI writing policy, 2026. The principles are theirs. The wording
> and the vault-specific rules are mine.

Good writing moves an idea out of one head and into another head, clearly.

AI models write fluent text. They do not yet write text you can ship without reading it. As the
author, you take the time to confirm that every idea in the piece is an idea you meant to
convey. That includes the structure and the emphasis, because the order of the ideas is what
decides which ones the reader remembers.

Use AI to brainstorm, to draft, and to proofread. Then apply the five principles below.

## 1. Stand behind every sentence

You own each idea and each sentence in the document before you share it. "The AI wrote that
line, ignore it" is not an answer to a reviewer. A reader who finds one sentence you did not
mean starts to doubt the other ones. So read the whole thing as if you typed it, because from
the reader's side you did.

## 2. Writing is thinking

The work of deciding what to emphasise is the work of understanding the topic. Skip it and you
finish with a document and no new knowledge. Specs, status updates and retrospectives are
proof of thought, so the artifact is only half the point. Even when AI helps you think, you
understand the problem better after you review the result line by line.

## 3. Spend more time writing than the reader spends reading

A short prompt that becomes a long document moves the cost onto every reader. They can prompt a
model themselves if they want volume. One person paying a one-time cost to cut and sharpen
saves every reader a repeated cost. That trade is always worth it.

## 4. Longer is not better

Length is the easiest thing for a model to add and the hardest thing for a reader to forgive.
A long document hides the real content inside sentences that say nothing. When the piece came
from a short prompt, ask whether the prompt itself is the better artifact.

There is no lossless way to expand natural language. Every rewrite changes the meaning, and the
thing doing the rewrite does not hold your actual intent. Readers want your thoughts, even
rough. Polish that costs information is a bad trade.

## 5. Mark raw AI output as raw

You can quote AI text that fails these standards, as long as you label it. "Claude suggested
this, do you think it is worth a look?" is honest and useful. Passing it off as your own
finished thought is what this policy exists to stop.

## How this gets enforced

1. Read the piece end to end before you send it. No exceptions for short pieces.
2. Run `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and take CRIT to 0.
3. Cut the document until every paragraph earns its place. Cutting beats adding.
4. When you cannot defend a sentence, delete it rather than rewrite it.

The scorer catches the words. This file catches the reason. A piece can score 0 and still break
this policy, because a clean sentence you did not mean to write is still a sentence you did not
mean to write.

## Related

- [Write Simply](./core/write-simply.md) turns principles 2, 3 and 4 into a working method. It
  carries the plain-style rules, and the test that a sentence which reads badly usually means the
  idea under it is wrong. Always loaded, so it applies to every draft.
- [Runtime contract](./core/runtime-contract.md), the load order (the sequence rule files load in) and the checks.

# Net New Value

> **Purpose:** This file decides whether an idea is worth drafting at all. The other core files
> decide how the draft reads. It loads for every channel: LinkedIn, X, Substack Notes, Substack
> articles and anything else Atharva publishes. Adapted from a creator post Atharva saved on
> 2026-09-25. The two-by-two grid is theirs. The application to this vault is his.

## Only Box 4 Ships, on Every Channel

Every insight sits on two axes. Is it obvious to the reader, or new to them? Is it tactical, so
the reader can act on it today, or is it only an idea?

| | Non-tactical | Tactical |
|---|---|---|
| **Obvious** | Box 1. The reader ignores it. | Box 2. The reader skims it, because it confirms what they believe. |
| **Non-obvious** | Box 3. The reader repeats it to a friend and does nothing. | **Box 4, Net New Value.** The reader saves it and uses it the same day. |

Net New Value means box 4: an insight the reader has not heard, with a step they can take now.

The source uses a sleep coach to show all four boxes. Box 1 is "get more rest". Box 2 is "sleep 8
hours a night". Box 3 is "you build up sleep debt even when you feel fine". Box 4 is the coffee nap.
The reader drinks a coffee, naps for 20 minutes, and wakes up as the caffeine takes effect.

The same grid in Atharva's own field reads like this.

1. Box 1. "Use AI carefully in your writing."
2. Box 2. "Put your writing rules in CLAUDE.md."
3. Box 3. "Most rules in a CLAUDE.md never reach the draft."
4. Box 4. "Put the rule in a PostToolUse hook, a script Claude Code runs after each file write.
   Let it run the scorer and return `decision: block`, so a draft with a CRIT cannot save." This is
   how `.claude/hooks/writing-gate.py` works.

## Run the Test Before the First Line

Write the insight as one sentence before you draft. Then answer three questions in writing.

1. Which box is it in? Say the box number.
2. What does the reader do in the next two minutes because of this piece? Name the exact action.
3. Where have they already heard it? If the answer is "every other account in the niche", it is
   box 1 or box 2, however well it is phrased.

A box 4 insight goes to the channel skill. Anything else gets one upgrade attempt, then it goes back
to the idea bank.

## Upgrade the Box by Adding the Missing Axis

A box below 4 lacks one axis or both. The fix is to add the axis that is missing.

1. Box 3 has the surprise and lacks the step. Add the exact command, number, tool name or order of
   operations that turns the fact into an action.
2. Box 2 has the step and lacks the surprise. Find what Atharva's own build showed that the common
   advice gets wrong, and lead with that.
3. Box 1 lacks both. Cut it. Polish on a box 1 idea produces a well-written post that nobody saves.

A long article can carry box 2 and box 3 material as setup. The headline claim and every section's
claim must still be box 4, or the article is a summary of the field.

## New Packaging Counts, Invented Facts Do Not

The source reports a client who gained 10,000 followers from one post. She learned nothing new for
it. She packaged what she already knew in a form her readers had never seen. So box 4 usually comes
from Atharva's own builds, numbers and mistakes, which no other account has.

The fabrication rule in `core/runtime-contract.md` still holds. Never invent a number, a result or a
step to push an idea into box 4. When the tactical detail is missing, ask Atharva for it or mark the
gap as `[the real step]`.

  that run after the draft exists
- [World](../World.md), what the piece is for

# Write Simply

> **Purpose:** `core/pattern-rules.md` says what to cut. This file says what to aim for, and how
> to tell when a draft got there. Loaded on every writing job, right after the pattern rules.
>
> Distilled from three Paul Graham essays: [Write Simply](https://paulgraham.com/simply.html),
> [Good Writing](https://paulgraham.com/goodwriting.html) and
> [Writes and Write-Nots](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html). The observations are his. The rules
> and the vault wiring are mine.

## 1. Simple is the default, complex is a decision

Use ordinary words and short sentences. Keep the technical term and simplify every word around it.

A complicated sentence written on purpose is a tool. A complicated sentence written by accident is
clumsy. Both look the same on the page, so the writer is the only person who can tell them apart.
Never write one by accident.

This rule also protects a draft. An edit that flattens a deliberate long sentence has broken
something, so read the intent before you cut.

## 2. Every sentence spends the reader's energy

A reader arrives with a fixed amount of attention. Energy spent on your prose is energy that never
reaches your idea.

Most readers quit part way through a long piece. Lower friction means more of them finish. That is
the entire return on an hour of cutting.

Fancy writing moves work onto the reader so the writer looks clever. Do not charge them for that.

**What changed in 2026.** The reader now has a model open in the next tab. Ask it your question and
it answers in four sentences, with no warm-up and no history of the field. That is the piece your
draft competes against, and it costs the reader nothing to switch.

So the price of a slow opening moved. It used to cost a little attention. It now costs the whole
reader, because the shorter version already exists and sits one keystroke away. The same holds for
a padded middle and for a term you left unexplained. A reader who has to guess stops guessing and
asks the model instead.

Three faults are fatal now, in this order. The piece takes too long to reach its claim. The piece
buries the claim under qualifiers and clauses. The piece uses a word the reader does not have.
`SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` checks all three: `slow-lede` for the first, `padded` for the second,
`undefined-term` for the third.

What survives is the part a model cannot produce: the number you measured, the thing you tried that
failed, the decision you made and the reason. Write those first and cut toward them.

## 3. A hard topic does not license hard words

Many readers do not read English first. Their grasp of the idea often runs ahead of their grasp of
the language. Write plainly because the subject is hard. Difficulty never grants permission to stop.

The same choice buys durability. A reader ten years from now sits in the same position as a foreign
reader today, because the language and the references will have moved.

## 4. Plain prose is an honesty test

Complicated writing hides missing ideas, and some writers pick it for that reason. Say nothing
simply and everyone sees it, including you.

So when a sentence resists becoming plain, inspect the idea before you inspect the words. The
resistance is usually the idea, and no rewrite fixes an idea that is not there.

## 5. A sentence that sounds wrong usually means the idea is wrong

Prose that reads well is more likely to be right. The mechanism is simple. You will never rewrite
an awkward passage into a version you believe less, so any forced change moves toward what you
actually meant.

State the claim in the safe direction. Good sound proves internal consistency rather than truth,
because a careful liar also sounds good. Read the signal the other way instead. A passage that
reads badly almost always carries a broken idea inside it.

The diagnostic is one question. When a line reads badly, do not reach for a synonym. Ask what you
meant to say there.

This holds for writing that develops an idea. It does not hold for a piece that reports finished
work, such as a release note or a build report, where the thinking already happened elsewhere.

## 6. Two edits that improve a draft with no new thinking

**Force a length change.** Take one paragraph and make it a line shorter. The constraint is
arbitrary and the result still improves, because a rewrite cannot move away from what you meant.
Use it on any paragraph you cannot fix by argument.

**Read as the first reader.** The writer reads the draft more times than anybody else will. Read it
cold and mark every place where something catches. Then repair the idea at that spot, not the word.

## 7. Rhythm follows the idea, never a meter

Good rhythm is not regular. A simple idea gets a short sentence. A subtle idea needs a long one to
carry its conditions.

An even cadence is therefore a defect, and so is a clipped sentence added for punch. Never
regularise a draft, and never truncate one.

## 8. Writing is thinking, so keep the thinking

Leslie Lamport put the stake plainly: "If you're thinking without writing, you only think you're
thinking."

AI removed most of the pressure to write. The population now splits into writers and non-writers,
which is the same line as the split between thinkers and non-thinkers.

This is the villain in [World](../World.md) wearing a new coat. Handing a draft to a model whole is
renting the thinking. Use a model to draft, to argue and to check. Keep every decision about what
the piece claims.

## 9. The reader was not in the room

Every term has a first appearance. That is the sentence where the reader either
keeps reading or starts guessing.

Guessing costs more than stopping. A reader who stops looks the word up and
comes back right. A reader who guesses reads the next ten paragraphs against
the wrong definition and never finds out.

Two kinds of word cause this, and only one of them is your problem to fix.

**A borrowed term** is real industry vocabulary. `webhook`, `context window`,
`fine-tune`. A reader who searches for one gets the correct answer in a click.
Leave it bare and the reader takes one detour.

**An owned term** is one this vault coined, or bent to a private meaning.
`harness`, `load order`, `state file`, `flywheel`, `second brain`,
`digital twin`, `ICP`. A reader who searches for one of these gets somebody
else's definition and walks away confidently wrong. The internet cannot rescue
that. Only your page can.

So an owned term carries its meaning where it first appears. Four shapes do the
job, and the scorer accepts all four.

| Shape | Example |
|---|---|
| Copula | a harness is everything you build around the model |
| Naming clause | a hook, which is a script that runs on its own |
| Parenthetical | the load order (the sequence those files arrive in) |
| Concepts table | `\| Harness \| Everything around the model \| You own this part \|` |

For a piece that leans on four or more owned terms, put the concepts table
before the argument. Rule 10 in
[Long-Form Writing Rules](../Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) already asks for
this on unfamiliar areas, and it costs the reader twenty seconds.

Numbers break the same rule from the other side. A paragraph carrying four
separate figures hands the reader nothing to hold, so none of them land. Rule 4
of the same file asks for a number per claim. Four numbers in one breath is one
wall, not four claims.

Run the check. `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"`, and CRIT reaches 0.
A hook blocks the write while it does not, because this is the rule a tired
writer skips first.

**Where this came from.** On 2026-09-04 a batch of 49 pieces cleared slop CRIT 0,
LinkedIn format CRIT 0 and SEO 0, and a reader outside the meeting still could
not follow one of them. Every gate measured the words. None of them asked whether
the reader had been handed the words first.

## 10. The pass

Run this with the section 7 checklist in `core/pattern-rules.md`, after the scorer reaches CRIT 0.

- [ ] Read one paragraph aloud. Does any sentence use a word a smart non-native reader would stop on?
- [ ] Find the most complicated sentence in the draft. Was it a decision, or an accident?
- [ ] Find the sentence that reads worst. Fix the idea under it rather than the wording.
- [ ] Take the weakest paragraph and cut it by one line. Keep the shorter version unless it lost a fact.
- [ ] Read the sentence lengths across one section. Is the cadence even enough to feel machine set?
- [ ] Name the decision in this piece that came from you and not from the model. If none exists, stop.
- [ ] List every owned term in the draft. Does each one carry its meaning where it first appears?
- [ ] Find the paragraph with the most figures in it. Can a reader hold all of them?
- [ ] Read the first 40 words alone. Do they carry a figure, a name, a command, or the reader?
- [ ] Ask what a model would answer in four sentences. Does your draft add anything past that?

## Related

- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the load order and the checks
- [Pattern rules](./pattern-rules.md), the failure shapes a regex cannot catch
- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive
- [World](../World.md), the villain and the skill tree
- [Voice](../Voice.md), how the writing sounds

# World

Three files decide how the writing sounds. This one decides what it is for. Every article, post, Note and tweet moves one reader one step away from the villain and toward the vision. A piece that does neither has no reason to exist.

Derived from 80 published articles, 145 posted LinkedIn posts and 53 tweets. The evidence sits in [Brand World Derivation 2026-08-25](../INBOX/Reports/Brand%20World%20Derivation%202026-08-25.md).

## The villain: rented work

Rented work is work you do not keep. You pay for it in hours or in dollars, it produces a result once, and it leaves nothing behind that works for you tomorrow. The bill arrives again next month and the asset never does.

[Principles](./Principles.md) already stated this rule in 2026-02: rent no platforms. The villain is that rule inverted and applied to the reader's whole week.

Three symptoms a reader recognizes in their own calendar:

1. A weekly report eats 30 minutes every Friday, and it has eaten 30 minutes every Friday for two years.
2. One post reaches 40,000 people, and the next eleven reach 300, because the reach belonged to the platform.
3. A process lives in one person's head, so the process stops when that person takes leave.

The word `compound` appears 108 times across 17 published articles. Rented work is what happens when nothing compounds.

### The main symptom: vibes

In 2026 the fastest way to rent your work is to stop thinking. Copy the prompt, accept the first output, ship it, and repeat forever. The tool got stronger and the operator got weaker, so the output belongs to the vendor. The word `vibe` appears 90 times across 19 published articles, always as a criticism.

In 2026 the fastest way to rent your work is to stop thinking. Copy the prompt, accept the first output, ship it, and repeat forever. The tool got stronger and the operator got weaker, so the output belongs to the vendor. The word `vibe` appears 90 times across 19 published articles, always as a criticism.

## The vision: the owned system

The reader builds the system that does their work. It runs when they are asleep, it improves every time they touch it, and it belongs to them when they change employers. Every hour of work adds to something that was already there.

The proof is the two-week test. A stranger opens the repo, reads no chat history, asks no questions, and keeps the whole operation running for two weeks. Pass that test and the system is owned. Fail it and the system was you.

## The main character

A technical operator between 24 and 35 who already shipped something real. A docs site, a product, a small audience, or a job at a startup that trusted them with scope. They are good at the work and their output still resets every Monday. Nothing they built last quarter does anything for them this quarter.

They watch models absorb the exact tasks they built a career on. They cannot tell whether to go deeper or go wider, so they go faster instead.

## What is at stake

By the end of 2027, most of the tasks in their job description run without them. They either own a system by then, or they compete on speed against a machine. The window is roughly 18 months from 2026-08-25.

## The skill tree

Each pillar in [Content Pillars](./Content%20Pillars.md) teaches part of the escape. A piece of content earns its place by advancing one node.

### Pillar 1, AI and Applied AI

- The reader learns to question a default output instead of shipping it.
- The reader gives an agent memory, so it stops starting from zero.
- The reader encodes judgment into files, so the judgment survives the session.
- The reader builds a gate that refuses bad work, rather than a reminder that asks nicely.

### Pillar 2, DevRel and Technical Writing

- The reader replaces a repeated ritual with a tool they own.
- The reader writes documentation a stranger can follow with no follow-up question.
- The reader restructures code so an agent can work on it safely.
- The reader owns the pipe to every platform they publish on.

### Pillar 3, Growth and Content Systems

- The reader builds distribution once and reuses it, rather than posting into the void.
- The reader refreshes an existing asset before writing a new one.
- The reader measures citations and shares, not impressions.
- The reader runs a content system that ships without the reader present.

## The vocabulary

The list holds eight terms. A term earns its place by appearing in the work already, never by being coined in a strategy document. Counts come from article bodies in `SUBSTACK/2_PUBLISHED/`.

| Term | What it means | Body hits |
|---|---|---|
| Rented work | Work you pay for repeatedly and never own | new, the villain |
| The owned system | A system that runs when you are away | new, the vision |
| The two-week test | A stranger runs your operation for two weeks | new, the proof |
| Compound | Every hour of work adds to yesterday's work | 108 |
| Vibes | Using a tool without thinking about the output | 90 |
| Flywheel | One piece of work that feeds the next piece | 47 |
| Digital twin | Identity files an agent reads to act as you | 15 |
| AI slop | Machine-shaped prose a scorer can measure | 13 |

Three terms are new and five are established. Use the new three until they earn their own counts, then check this table again. Drop `second brain`, because Tiago Forte owns it. `Brutalist efficiency` sits in [Principles](./Principles.md) and appears in zero articles, so either use it or stop listing it.

## How to use this file

1. Name the villain or the vision in the first 100 words of any long-form piece.
2. Name the skill-tree node the piece advances, before you write a line.
3. Use a vocabulary term where a generic word would fit, and never invent a ninth term mid-draft.
4. State the season and beat from the current season file, or say the piece sits outside the season.

A piece that cannot name a node is an idea, not an article. Send it back to `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS/`.

# Technical Writing Style Guide

## The five rules that matter most

Read these first. They are the whole guide in five lines, and they are non-negotiable on every piece this
repo publishes. Everything below is the detail behind them.

1. **No clever declarative sentences.** If a quotable-sounding line has no fact you can point at, cut it.
   Keep the number, drop the flourish. ("The fourth row settles it" is out.)
2. **Name every referent.** No dangling noun. "All four write SQL" and "the best editor of the four" make
   the reader ask "four what". Name the thing in the sentence that uses it.
3. **Exact number or plain scope, never a vague count.** "13+ data platforms" makes the reader ask "is that
   14 or 200". Say "any data platform or cloud database", or a real number.
4. **One idea per sentence, and no contradiction.** Do not fuse two facts into one sentence, and never let a
   sentence contradict the one before it.
5. **Write two reading levels down. This is not marketing copy.** Keep the technical terms, simplify the
   words around them. Dry, accurate, concise.

The test that finds all five: read a sentence and ask "what are you trying to say?", then say that in fewer,
smaller words. Also cut any filler transition and any sentence whose subject is the article, the table or the
paragraph. Inform, do not narrate.

Section 0 is the full reader-first list, section 2 has the worked before-and-after examples.

---

**Scope: every word this repo publishes.** Listicles, product highlights, blog posts, landing-page copy,
docs and release notes all follow this file. Load it before you write or edit any of them.

Three sources feed it and they do not conflict: the freeCodeCamp publication style guide (vendored at
`content/listicles/review/sources/freecodecamp-publication-style-guide.md`), the Altimate tone-of-voice guide
at `altimate-marketing-os/about-company-context/brand-messaging/tone-of-voice.md`, and the machine-checked
slop rules in `D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\slop\slop_rules.py`.


**The freeCodeCamp guide is a fallback, and its contents are guidelines rather than rules.** It is somebody
else's house style, written for a different publication and a different audience. Consult it where this file
is silent, and treat what it says as a sensible default rather than a requirement. Where it disagrees with
this file or with the tone-of-voice guide, those win and no note is needed. Nothing in it is enforced by a
gate, and no review should cite it as grounds for a change.

## 1. Sentence shapes

**The copula dodge.** A model replaces `is` with `serves as`, `stands as`, `represents`, `marks`,
`boasts`, `features` or `offers`. The mechanism is a repetition penalty. The model avoids reusing
the common word `is`, and the substitute implies a relationship that does not exist. Write `is`.
Keep `serves as` only where a real function sits beyond plain identity.

**Tacked-on analysis.** A participle clause bolted to the end of a sentence to fake depth. The
shapes are `highlighting its importance`, `underscoring the shift`, `reflecting a broader trend`
and `marking a significant moment`. These clauses carry no new fact. They claim the fact before
them matters and supply no evidence. Cut the clause. If the significance is real, write it as its
own sentence with its own proof.

**Unearned significance.** A claim of impact, legacy or scale with no support in the same
paragraph. Watch for `a pivotal moment`, `a key turning point`, `setting the stage for` and
`an enduring legacy`. Training data rewards important-sounding prose, so the
model asserts importance and expects the evidence to arrive later. State only what the evidence
carries. Real significance falls out of the evidence on its own.

**The courtroom noun.** A judgment word standing in for a result nobody adjudicated. `verdict` is the
current one, and it arrives as `so the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation`
or as `the verdict is still out`. The same move hides in `ruling`, `the jury is out`, `case closed`,
`indictment` and `exonerates`. Two things break at once. The noun is a metaphor doing the work of a
number, and the `not a verdict, it's Y` frame negates a word the reader never proposed, which is the
banned antithesis with a straw man inside it. Write the result, the number, or the reason you cannot
tell yet. Keep the word where a real decision with named values exists, such as a court, or software
that emits one.

**Vague authority.** A claim attributed to an unnamed group. `Experts agree`, `studies suggest`,
`research shows`, `observers note` and `industry reports indicate` all simulate a source. Name the
expert, link the study, or drop the claim. There is no third option.

**The false range.** A `from X to Y` span where X and Y do not sit on one spectrum. The sentence
`From innovation to cultural change, AI is rewriting everything` reads as coverage and states
nothing. Name the two or three real things.

**Name-dropping.** A list of outlets, tools or names with no fact attached. `Featured in Forbes,
TechCrunch and Wired` names sources and says nothing. The model lists authority to borrow it. Pick
one name and say what it said, or cut the list.

**Abstract metaphor nouns.** A concrete idea dressed as a technical term. The set is `substrate`,
`vector` used for a way, `locus`, `vantage`, `nexus`, `bedrock`, `modality` and `endgame`. Each one
reads as precise and hides a plainer word: `base`, `way`, `place`, `last phase`. Pick the plain
word. His own working terms are exempt, because he chose them on purpose. `harness`, `flywheel`,
`scaffolding`, `surface` and `primitive` stay. The precedence ladder in the runtime contract
settles any other case, and it favours his voice.

**The aphorism formula.** An ordinary claim dressed as reusable wisdom. The shapes are
`X is the currency of Y`, `the architecture of X` and `X becomes a trap`. This sounds
profound and loses the fact. Rule 23 in `slop_rules.py` bans the clever one-liner. This is the
same failure with a formula behind it, so replace the formula with the concrete claim under it.

**The theatrical opener.** A standalone `Honestly?`, `Look,`, `Real talk` or `Here is the thing`
placed before an ordinary point. The tell is the fake reveal, because a person being honest just
says the thing. The same words mid-sentence in casual prose are ordinary English, so read the
position and not the word.

**Adverbs propping up weak verbs.** `He ran very quickly` hides `he sprinted`. When the adverb is
load-bearing, the verb is wrong. Replace the verb and delete the adverb.

**Elegant variation.** The model renames its subject to avoid repeating it, so one person becomes
`the researcher`, then `the prominent figure`, then `the key player`. Rule 28 says one word for one
thing. This is the mechanism it defends against. Repeat the real name.

## 2. Paragraph and section shapes

**False balance.** The three-step formula runs positive framing, then a nod at problems, then
instant dismissal. `Despite these challenges, the opportunity is enormous` is the shape of
analysis with none of the work. Engage the problem and let it stand, or drop the pretence.

**Tricolon saturation.** The rule of three is a real device and a model reaches for it by default,
because three items look thorough with no need to be thorough. One tricolon per paragraph, never
two in a row. Four real items get listed as four. Two real items get written as prose.

**The outline wrapper.** Section titles that a template chose rather than the content. The set is
`Challenges and future directions`, `Key takeaways`, `Legacy and impact`, `Overview` and
`Background`. Each one announces generation before a reader reads a word. Rule 4 in `Voice.md`
already demands a heading that states a conclusion, so name what the section delivers.

**Fractal recapping.** A summary before a section starts, and another after it ends. Both
`In this section we will cover` and `as we have seen` are padding inherited from textbooks. Rule 15
bans the trailing summary, and this rule bans the leading one. Write forward.

**Diff-anchored writing.** Prose that narrates a change instead of describing the thing. The line
`This section replaces the old onboarding flow` only makes sense to a reader who saw the old one. A
changelog, a release note and a migration guide are version-scoped by nature and are exempt.
Everything else reads coherently to a reader who arrived today.

**One-point dilution.** The same claim restated ten times across four thousand words, sold as depth.
Say the claim once. Then spend the length on evidence, on the counterargument, and on what follows.

**The undone claim.** A later line quietly reverses an earlier one. The hook promises a result and the
close hedges it. A post says "about thirty minutes" and its pinned comment says "under one hour". Each
line reads fine alone, so the writer is the least likely person to see it. Read line 1 against line 2,
line 2 against the body, the ending against the opening, and the pinned comment against the post. Fix
the weaker line and leave the stronger one. Never rewrite both.

**The echo stack.** Three or more consecutive lines built on one skeleton, such as "The page lacks X.
There is no Y. Z does not exist." The model repeats the last structure it wrote, and a person
escalates. Make each line add a fact or raise the cost, keep the strongest, and put the rest in one
list whose items differ in shape. Swapping synonyms into the same skeleton keeps the echo.

## 3. Fill that is not content

**Assistant bleed.** The set is `I hope this helps`, `Certainly`, `Would you like me to`,
`Feel free to adjust` and `Here is a draft of`. Each one belongs in a chat window, and inside a
deliverable each one is contamination. Start with the content.

**Cutoff disclaimers.** The set is `As of my last update`, `while specific details are limited`
and `based on available information`. Each one is a hedge formatted as content. Say the honest
thing once instead, or ask him.

**Placeholder leakage.** An unfilled field that ships. `[insert link]`, `INSERT_SOURCE_URL`,
`access-date 2026-XX-XX` and `add image if available` all reach the reader when nobody re-read the
draft. A bracket from the fabrication rule is deliberate and stays visible on purpose. A bracket
from a template is a defect.

**Promotional register.** The set is `nestled`, `in the heart of`, `vibrant`, `boasts`, `renowned`
and `a diverse array`. All of it comes from tourism copy and press releases. Write the neutral
declarative version instead.
Rule 8 in `Voice.md` says the same thing from the other side, so say what the thing does.

## 4. Formatting tells

**Em dash density.** Already CRIT in `slop_rules.py`, so this is the reason behind that ban. Model
output uses the em dash far above human rates and puts it where a comma belongs. Do not trade the em
dash for parentheses or an en dash. That move swaps one tell for another. End the sentence, or use a
comma.

**The colon as a connector.** A colon that joins two clauses mid-sentence fakes a cause. The line
`The fix is simple: you rewrite the query` adds nothing that a period would not. A colon is correct
before a list or an example. Everywhere else, end the sentence. Rule 17 in `slop_rules.py` already
bans a colon in a heading, and this is the same tell inside a line.

**Bold on every key phrase in running prose.** Emphasis stops meaning anything once it is
everywhere. Reserve bold for a term you are defining, or for a label that opens a line. Rule 2 in
`Voice.md` sets the boundary per folder. A bold label must earn its place with a new fact after it.
`**Performance:** Performance improved 40%` fails, because the label only repeats the line.
`**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file` passes, because the detail is new.

**Sentence case in an H2.** Every H2 uses AP Title Case, in every channel, and states the claim
its section proves. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` blocks a miscased H2 and flags a topic label.
H1 and H3 and below keep the case their destination uses. A model that capitalises every word of
an H3 or a body label is still showing the old tell.

**A skipped heading level, or a rule above every heading.** Jumping H2 to H4, or dropping `---`
before each section by reflex, are both template tics. Neither is a writing choice.

## 5. What to leave alone

Sections 1 to 4 are a list of things to remove. Applied without judgement they produce the second
failure, which is prose stripped so hard that nobody is home. That output is not human. It is a
different machine's output, and it is the source of every complaint that edited writing reads flat,
boring and sanded down.

**None of the following is evidence of AI on its own.** Do not cut one unless it sits in a cluster
with real tells.

- Clean grammar and a consistent style. Many writers are edited. Polish proves nothing.
- Formal vocabulary. The banned list names specific overused words. It does not ban intelligence.
  Leave "ostensibly", "notwithstanding" and "constituent" where they are the right word.
- A mix of casual and formal register. That usually marks a technical writer, not a chatbot.
- Dry, plain prose. For a runbook it is correct.
- One transition word. A single "however" is English. The pile-up is the tell.
- One short emphatic sentence. People land points with a clipped sentence. Flag the drumbeat only
  when several stack up and inflate the tone.
- A salutation or a sign-off. Letters are older than chatbots.
- An unsourced claim. Most writing is unsourced. That is a rigor problem and not an AI problem.
- A watched word inside a quotation, a title, a proper noun or an example. When the piece discusses
  the phrase rather than uses it, leave it exactly as written.

## 6. What to protect

Removing tells is half the job. The other half is leaving alive whatever was already alive. These
are the hardest things for a model to produce and the easiest for an eager edit to erase.

- **Odd, specific, hard-to-invent detail.** A real address. A strange quote. "The lawyer who worked
  upstairs from my dentist." Models round specifics off and people hoard them. Never generalise one
  of these to make a sentence flow.
- **Mixed feelings left unresolved.** "I think this is mostly right and it still bothers me." A
  model defaults to a clean take. Do not resolve the tension for him.
- **Dated references.** Slang, a meme, an in-joke anchored to one year and one subculture. Models
  lag by a year, so these are strong human signal.
- **A genuine aside or a self-correction.** A parenthesis where the writer interrupts himself.
  Machines rarely do that.
- **Uneven rhythm.** A nine-word sentence next to a forty-word one. Model output drifts toward one
  uniform mid-length cadence. The variance is the signal, so never regularise it.
- **An opinion he can defend.** If he can say why he chose a word, that reasoning outranks every
  rule in this file.
- **A deliberate quirk.** A writer who always opens lowercase, or never uses a semicolon, is doing
  something. Match it.

**The operating principle is clusters, not instances.** One em dash means nothing. An em dash plus
a tricolon plus "vibrant tapestry" plus a "Challenges" heading is a confession.

When you cannot tell whether something is his voice or a machine default, the precedence ladder in
the runtime contract decides it. Assume it is his, and leave it.

**When a draft carries none of the signals in section 6, the problem is not that AI patterns
remain.** The problem is that nobody is home. Adding a specific, a stance and some unevenness beats
deleting one more banned word. The fabrication rule sets the limit on how a specific gets added.
It comes from him, never from invention.

## 7. The pass before you hand it over

Run this after the scorer reaches CRIT 0, because the scorer cannot see any of it.

- [ ] Any "serves as" or "represents a" standing in for "is"?
- [ ] Any tacked-on participle claiming significance?
- [ ] Any impact claim with no evidence beside it?
- [ ] Any unnamed authority carrying a fact?
- [ ] Two tricolons in a row, or a tricolon that hides four real items?
- [ ] A template heading, a leading recap, or a trailing recap?
- [ ] Any assistant bleed, cutoff hedge or leftover placeholder?
- [ ] Any colon joining two clauses where a period belongs?
- [ ] Any bold label that only repeats the line after it?
- [ ] Any metaphor noun where a plain word fits, outside his working terms?
- [ ] Any list of names or outlets with no fact attached?
- [ ] Any fact, name, number or source that he did not supply?
- [ ] Does any later line undo an earlier one? Read the hook against line 2, the body against the pinned comment, and the ending against the opening.
- [ ] Cover everything after the opening. Can you still guess how the piece ends? If so, the hook answered itself.
- [ ] Did anything from section 5 get cut that should have stayed?
- [ ] Did every signal in section 6 survive the edit?
- [ ] List every heading in the draft on one line. Does any heading state an outline slot rather than a claim, so it would sit unchanged over a different topic?
- [ ] Find the one sentence in the draft that only Atharva could have written: a real date, a named person, a number from his own work, a moment he was wrong. If no such sentence exists, the draft is not done.
- [ ] If the piece covers several parallel items, read only the closing line of each one in a row. Do they all sound interchangeable with the nouns swapped?

## 7b. Fixing a MED without creating the next one
## 0. The reader-first rules, non-negotiable

Set by the owner on 19 Aug 2026 after reading the listicle cluster line by line. These outrank taste and
apply to every piece this repo publishes, not only listicles. Several are elaborated in the numbered sections
below and are repeated here because a reviewer reads this list first. Where a rule points at a section, that
section is the detail.

1. **Write plain English.** No flowery sentences, ever. This is the rule the other fourteen serve.
2. **No metaphors and no rhetorical flourish.** Say the literal action. A term of art with an agreed meaning (blast radius, fan-out, guardrail) is not a metaphor and stays.
3. **Never write a sentence about the article.** No "a table follows", "read this with that in mind", "here is the honest limit". Inform, do not narrate. See section 2.
4. **No self-criticism as a hook.** Do not lead with our own weakness, stage it as a reveal, or give it a heading. State a real limit plainly when the reader needs it, then move on.
5. **No bragging.** Do not tell the reader how special we are ("the data nobody else publishes"). Show the number and let it speak.
6. **No unstructured statistic dumps.** A run of numbers is a table or a bullet list, or it does not go in.
7. **Headings tell, they do not tease.** The reader must know what the section covers from the heading alone. No curiosity teasers, bare noun phrases, count riddles, dangling pronouns or aphorisms. Do not bury the lede. See section 4.
8. **Every compared item gets the same block, in the same order:** what it is, who it is for, who uses it today, the features, the pricing, what it lacks. The reader compares across items, not across four different essays.
9. **Use bullets with a bold label, then expand.** One bullet per attribute, label first. Do not bury an attribute mid-paragraph: a reader comparing several items reads down the bold labels to find the one they care about, and cannot do that if pricing is a bullet under one item and a clause under the next.
10. **Comparison tables use marks, not words.** A tick, a cross, or a hyphen for none, with a short qualifier beside the mark. Never "Yes / No / none published".
11. **Lead with use case, not benchmarks.** Fit and features are the main focus, score is secondary evidence, never the structure of the piece.
12. **Cut corporate trivia, but reference solution owners or maintainers.** No mergers, acquisitions, funding rounds or valuations. A data engineer choosing a tool does not care.  Do mention the organization behind a tool or open source project.
13. **Publish the figure, not its provenance.** Drop "who ran it", the provenance and the benchmark dates as details in the running text. Keep the number and its just link to its source.
14. **Write for the reader, not for yourself or an internal team mate.** No leaked internal identifiers, no "that third line is why...", nothing that makes them scroll back to follow the point.
15. **Open with a real introduction.** Establish context quicly to orient the reader and confirm the topic. Start with the reader's situation, demonstrate empathy, show you can relate, then say what you compare and on what basis. Never jump straight into item one.
16. **Write plain, one or two reading levels down. This is not marketing copy.** Keep the technical terms and simplify the sentence around them. A working data engineer wants dry, accurate and concise. Ask yourself "what are we trying to say?", then say it in fewer, smaller words where possible, without patronizing our technically sophisticated audience. See section 2, "Kill the clever declarative".
17. **No clever or provocative declarative sentences.** Do not try to sound smart while teaching the reader nothing. Each sentence must convey value-adding information. Say the plain thing instead. See section 2.
18. **Name every noun the reader needs.** No dangling referent. "All four write competent SQL" and "the best editor of the four" make the reader stop and ask "all four what". Name them in the sentence. See section 2, "Name every referent".
19. **Give an exact figure or a plain scope, never a vague count.** "13+ data platforms" makes the reader ask "is that 14 or 200". Prefer a plain-English scope such as "any data platform or cloud database", or a real number. Where the site-wide naming rule requires the platform list, name the platforms and drop the "+N" framing.
20. **One idea per sentence, and no internal contradiction.** Do not fuse two separate claims into one sentenc. Split the ideas and confirm they agree.
21. **No courtroom noun where a result belongs.** Added 25 Aug 2026 on the owner's report. "Verdict" is the current offender, in "it's not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation" and in "the verdict is still out". State the result, the number or the reason you cannot tell. The shape is banned and the bare word is not, because Altimate Code's PR review really does emit a signed verdict. See section 11.

The brand-safety gate `S2-*` in `check-listicles.mjs` enforces the framing half of rules 3, 4 and 12 as an
advisory warning. It is a floor. This list is the bar.

---

## 1. Substance decides the article

## 10. No existence-assertions in place of claims

Never write that something "is real," "is genuine," "is legitimate," "isn't
just noise," or "is actually there."

That construction marks a spot where a specific claim belongs. Replace it with:
 - the number (effect size, magnitude, direction, sample, interval), or
 - the attribution ("three of five interviewees raised it"), or
 - a plain statement that you can't tell, and what would settle it.

Before finishing, scan the draft for this pattern and rewrite every instance.

Examples:
 "The difference in the data is real"
   → "Group B converted 4.1pp higher (12.7% vs 8.6%, n=1,840, p=.003)."
 "The difference in the data is real" [numbers unavailable]
   → "I can't separate that gap from variance at this sample size; it'd take
      roughly 2,000 sessions per arm."
 "The frustration is real"
   → cut the sentence, respond to the frustration.

Exception: technical senses of "real" are fine: real vs. nominal, real vs.
synthetic data, real numbers.

## 11. No courtroom nouns in place of a result

Reported by the owner on 25 Aug 2026 as the successor to the "is real" tic in section 10. It is the same
defect wearing a different word. A model reaches for a judgment noun where a plain result belongs, so the
sentence sounds decisive and tells the reader nothing.

The word to watch is **"verdict"**, and what is banned is the shape it arrives in, never the bare word. All
four of these are wrong:

- "So the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation."
- "It's not a verdict, it's a starting point."
- "The verdict on Fusion is still out."
- "That table delivers a verdict on both tools."

Two rules break at once. "Verdict" is a courtroom metaphor standing in for an ordinary analytic result,
which section 0 rule 2 bans. And "not a verdict, it's Y" negates a word the reader never proposed, which is
the banned "not X, it's Y" antithesis with a straw man inside it.

State the result instead.

| Rejected | Shipped |
|---|---|
| It's not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation. | Which tool costs less depends on your query volume. Under 400 queries a day, Altimate Code is cheaper. |
| The verdict on Fusion is still out. | dbt Labs has published no Fusion benchmark on a project this size, so we cannot compare the two yet. |
| That table delivers a verdict on both tools. | The table shows one tool failing 4 of the 12 checks and the other failing 1. |

The ban covers the rest of the courtroom set wherever it stands in for an assessment: "ruling", "the jury is
out", "case closed", "damning", "indictment", "exonerates" and "the evidence is in".

**The shape is banned and the bare word is not, which matters here more than anywhere else.** "Verdict" is a
real product noun on this site. Altimate Code's dbt PR review emits one signed verdict per pull request,
whose values are `APPROVE`, `COMMENT` and `REQUEST_CHANGES`, and seven articles use the word that way
correctly. It is also the citation-span field name (`VERIFIED`, `UNSOURCED`, `INFERRED`, `CONTRADICTED`) and
the label on a review-mode hover card. Banning the word itself would fail correct prose and push writers into
paraphrasing a term the product ships. Read the sentence, then ask whether an actual decision with named
values is being reported. If yes, keep the word. If it stands in for a result the writer owed the reader,
cut it and write the result.

## 12. Earn the insight before making the claim

Migrated from the tone-of-voice guide, which is where this rule used to live. It is article structure, so it
belongs here.

The reader has to understand the problem before the solution appears. Jumping to the product is the most
common structural failure in this corpus.

1. Name the problem a practitioner recognises from their own work.
2. Quantify or illustrate it, with a number, a scenario or a code example.
3. Say what the existing approaches miss.
4. Introduce what Altimate does differently, and be specific.

## 13. Say what breaks, not that something matters

Migrated from the tone-of-voice guide.

An adjective that ranks importance tells the reader you think a thing matters and never why, so they can
neither check you nor act on it. "Critical", "key", "core", "fundamental", "central", "the crux" and
"load-bearing" all do this. "Load-bearing" is also a metaphor, which rule 2 rules out: applied to a wall it is
literal, and applied to a term or a decision there is no structure and no load.

Name the dependency or the failure instead, which turns an assertion into something a reader can verify.
"Change it and competitor quotations render as callouts" is checkable. "That decision is load-bearing" is not.
If you cannot say what goes wrong without the thing, you do not yet know whether it matters.

## 14. Length and format by content type

Migrated from the tone-of-voice guide, which now covers only the surfaces this repo does not publish:
LinkedIn, press quotes and sales email.

| Content type | Length and format | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Listicle | 2,000 to 3,200 words, and the cap is a blocking gate. | Structure rules come from the listicle harness. |
| Blog post (concept or narrative) | 1,200 to 2,000 words. Section headers. One concrete CTA at the end. | Open on a practitioner scenario, not a market claim. End on a specific action. Prose in the body, not bullets. |
| Blog post (how-to or technical) | 800 to 1,500 words. Code blocks where relevant. Numbered step headers. | Start from a problem the reader has right now. Do not introduce Altimate until the problem is fully stated. |
| Product release notes | 50 to 200 words per feature: what it does, why it matters, how to use it. | Functional and direct. Engineers are reading this. |

# neatlogs Evidence

Every FirstRun run is one `firstrun.run` WORKFLOW trace in neatlogs. Its spans are `read_docs` and `step.<id>` (TOOL), `planner` and `recover.<id>` (AGENT), `classify_failure` (TOOL), and `budget` and `verify` (GUARDRAIL). Bisect adds `firstrun.bisect` with a `probe.<version>` span per release. Prerequisite Proof adds a `prereqs.prove` GUARDRAIL.

## Before and After Traces Measure the Fix From Neatlogs

| Target | v1 trace | v2 trace |
|---|---|---|
| neatlogs Python SDK | `fccdbad9a9c6177b90112911fe485bd6` | `495d510fd6da5546dbc6ab6e52bcee68` |
| Entire install | `10c44df9626c19f5ac801f1c6d84610e` | `5520c5cff5e0ea61f130eced082b20c4` |
| Chroma getting started | `66ec093b00333fa221fade5d2fc5f55f` | `f63d2b842c2257ae8c340f6ce44e3848` |
| OpenAI v0 README (fixture) | `b98b419e286acf436083febdb5217cf9` | `78e538e63a65c5d00d0281effa119567` |

Per-trace spans, tool calls, cost and duration are in [before_after_traces.json](before_after_traces.json). The tag summaries are in [neatlogs_runs.json](neatlogs_runs.json).

## One Failed-and-Recovered Trace, Exported

[trace-recovered-entire-v2.md](trace-recovered-entire-v2.md) is trace `5520c5cff5e0ea61f130eced082b20c4`. Step 1 failed with `curl: command not found`, recovery installed curl in the container, step 2 failed until `~/.local/bin` was on `PATH`, and a fresh container then ran all 4 steps with no model calls. The trace status reads ERROR because a failed step span rolls up to the trace, while the run itself ended `verified`.

    12	def _read() -> dict:
    13	    path = config.PRECEDENTS_FILE  # read at call time so tests can patch it
    14	    try:
    15	        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    16	    except OSError:
    17	        return {}

     3	from __future__ import annotations
     4	
     5	import hashlib
     6	import os
     7	import re

     9	import httpx
    10	import neatlogs

    12	from firstrun import config
    13	from firstrun.models import Classification, FailureClass
    14	
    15	JEV_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"
    16	JEV_MODEL = "jev-latest"
    17	
    18	# Usage of the last Claude fallback call. recovery.py adds it to the run, then clears it.
    19	LAST_USAGE: dict = {}
    20	
    21	_TELLING = re.compile(
    22	    r"error|exception|not found|failed|denied|no matching|cannot|can't|unable|unauthorized|refused|timed out|invalid|unknown|unrecognized",
    23	    re.I,
    24	)
    25	
    26	
    27	def signature(error_text: str) -> str:
    28	    """Short stable signature of an error: strips paths, numbers and hashes."""
    29	    lines = [ln.strip() for ln in error_text.splitlines() if ln.strip()]
    30	    telling = [ln for ln in lines if _TELLING.search(ln)]
    31	    line = (telling or lines or [""])[-1]  # tools print the real error last
    32	    line = line.lower()
    33	    line = re.sub(r"[\"'`]", "", line)
    34	    line = re.sub(r"(?:[a-z]:)?[\\/][^\s:,;)]*", "<path>", line)
    35	    line = re.sub(r"\b(?:0x)?[0-9a-f]{7,}\b", "<hex>", line)
    36	    line = re.sub(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)*", "<n>", line)
    37	    line = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", line).strip()
    38	    digest = hashlib.sha1(line.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]
    39	    prefix = re.sub(r"[^a-z]+", "-", line).strip("-")[:30].strip("-")
    40	    return f"{prefix}-{digest}" if prefix else digest
    41	
    42	
    43	def _normalize(raw: dict) -> dict[FailureClass, float]:
    44	    probs = {c: max(0.0, float(raw.get(c.value, 0.0) or 0.0)) for c in FailureClass}
    45	    total = sum(probs.values())
    46	    if total <= 0:
    47	        raise ValueError("no probabilities")
    48	    return {c: p / total for c, p in probs.items()}
    49	
    50	
    51	_CRITERIA = {
    52	    "docs_bug": "The docs are wrong: package renamed, flag removed, wrong import path, or a version that moved.",
    53	    "environment": "The sandbox is missing something: a system package in the base image, or a network timeout.",
    54	    "product_bug": "The tool itself crashes on a correct command.",
    55	    "needs_secret": "The step asks for an API key, token or login that the container lacks.",
    56	}

    59	def _jev(error_text: str, command: str) -> dict[FailureClass, float] | None:
    60	    """Ask Jev one Choice question. Returns None on any failure."""
    61	    config.load_env()
    62	    key = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY")
    63	    if not key:
    64	        return None
    65	    body = {
    66	        "model": JEV_MODEL,
    67	        "state": {"command": command, "error_output": error_text[-3000:]},
    68	        "questions": {"failure_class": {
    69	            "type": "choice",
    70	            "instructions": "A shell command from a quickstart guide failed in a clean container. Which kind of failure is it?",
    71	            "criteria": _CRITERIA,
    72	        }},
    73	    }
    74	    try:
    75	        r = httpx.post(JEV_URL, json=body, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}, timeout=30)
    76	        r.raise_for_status()
    77	        answer = r.json()["answers"]["failure_class"]
    78	        return _normalize(answer["probabilities"])
    79	    except Exception:  # any failure sends us to the next fallback
    80	        return None
    81	
    82	
    83	def _claude(error_text: str, command: str) -> dict[FailureClass, float] | None:
    84	    from firstrun import llm
    85	
    86	    prompt = (
    87	        "A shell command from a developer quickstart failed in a clean Docker container.\n"
    88	        f"Command: {command}\nError output:\n{error_text[-3000:]}\n\n"
    89	        "Classes: " + "; ".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in _CRITERIA.items()) + "\n"
    90	        'Return JSON: {"docs_bug": p, "environment": p, "product_bug": p, "needs_secret": p} '
    91	        "with probabilities that sum to 1."
    92	    )
    93	    try:
    94	        data, usage = llm.ask_json(prompt, system="You classify failures.", max_turns=1)
    95	        LAST_USAGE.clear()
    96	        LAST_USAGE.update(usage)
    97	        return _normalize(data)
    98	    except Exception:
    99	        return None
   100	
   101	
   102	# Ordered: the first matching group wins.
   103	_HEURISTICS: list[tuple[FailureClass, re.Pattern]] = [
   104	    (FailureClass.NEEDS_SECRET, re.compile(
   105	        r"api[_ -]?key|auth(?:entication|orization)? (?:required|failed|error)|unauthorized|\b401\b|"
   106	        r"not logged in|please log ?in|missing (?:token|credentials)|invalid (?:token|credentials)|(?-i:[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]+_(?:KEY|TOKEN|SECRET)\b)", re.I)),
   107	    (FailureClass.ENVIRONMENT, re.compile(
   108	        r"command not found|: not found|no such file or directory: '?(?:gcc|cc|make|git|curl)|"
   109	        r"could not resolve host|temporary failure in name resolution|timed out|connection (?:refused|reset)|"
   110	        r"failed to build wheel|error: command '(?:gcc|cc)' failed|python\.h|unable to locate package", re.I)),
   111	    (FailureClass.DOCS_BUG, re.compile(
   112	        r"no matching distribution|could not find a version|modulenotfounderror|importerror|cannot import name|"
   113	        r"unrecognized arguments|no such option|unknown (?:option|command|flag)|unexpected keyword|"
   114	        r"has no attribute|is not a known|deprecated|removed|404|no such command|invalid choice", re.I)),
   115	    (FailureClass.PRODUCT_BUG, re.compile(
   116	        r"segmentation fault|internal (?:server )?error|panic:|assertionerror|unhandled exception|core dumped|\b500\b", re.I)),
   117	]
   118	
   119	
   120	def _heuristic(error_text: str, command: str = "") -> dict[FailureClass, float]:
   121	    for cls, pattern in _HEURISTICS:
   122	        if pattern.search(error_text):
   123	            rest = 0.2 / 3
   124	            return {c: (0.8 if c == cls else rest) for c in FailureClass}
   125	    return {c: 0.25 for c in FailureClass}  # no signal: low confidence, so we ask
   126	
   127	
   128	@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="classify_failure")
   129	def classify(error_text: str, command: str = "") -> Classification:
   130	    """TOOL span `classify_failure`. Jev first, Claude as fallback. Returns four probabilities."""
   131	    config.assert_model_call_allowed("classification")
   132	    probs = _jev(error_text, command)
   133	    if probs is not None:
   134	        return Classification(probabilities=probs, source="jev")
   135	    neatlogs.log("jev unavailable, falling back to claude", level="warning")
   136	    probs = _claude(error_text, command)
   137	    if probs is not None:
   138	        return Classification(probabilities=probs, source="claude")
   139	    neatlogs.log("claude unavailable, falling back to heuristics", level="warning")
   140	    return Classification(probabilities=_heuristic(error_text, command), source="heuristic")

    13	from firstrun import budget as budget_mod

    29	CONFIDENT = 0.7        # below this, ask the human once
    30	STORE_CONFIDENT = 0.9  # at or above this, a model answer is stored as a precedent
    31	
    32	_LETTERS = {"d": FailureClass.DOCS_BUG, "e": FailureClass.ENVIRONMENT,
    33	            "p": FailureClass.PRODUCT_BUG, "s": FailureClass.NEEDS_SECRET}
    34	
    35	Asker = Callable[[str], str]
    36	
    37	ASK_TIMEOUT_S = 60  # the human has this long to answer the ask-once question
    38	
    39	
    40	class AskTimeout(Exception):
    41	    """A person sat at the terminal and gave no answer within ASK_TIMEOUT_S seconds."""
    42	
    43	
    44	class NeedsHuman(Exception):
    45	    """The human gave no answer. `classification` holds the model's best guess."""
    46	
    47	    def __init__(self, classification: Classification):
    48	        super().__init__("needs_human: no answer to the ask-once question")
    49	        self.classification = classification
    50	
    51	
    52	def _error_line(error_text: str) -> str:
    53	    lines = [ln.strip() for ln in error_text.splitlines() if ln.strip()]
    54	    return (lines[-1] if lines else "no output")[:200]
    55	
    56	
    57	def _terminal_asker(question: str) -> str | None:
    58	    """Ask in the terminal. No terminal returns None. No answer in ASK_TIMEOUT_S seconds raises AskTimeout."""
    59	    if not sys.stdin or not sys.stdin.isatty():
    60	        return None
    61	    box: list[str | None] = []
    62	
    63	    def read() -> None:
    64	        try:
    65	            box.append(input(question + " "))
    66	        except (EOFError, OSError):  # a console with no reader, such as a background job
    67	            box.append(None)
    68	
    69	    reader = threading.Thread(target=read, daemon=True)
    70	    reader.start()
    71	    reader.join(ASK_TIMEOUT_S)
    72	    if not box:
    73	        raise AskTimeout(f"no answer in {ASK_TIMEOUT_S} s")
    74	    return box[0]
    75	
    76	
    77	def _parse_answer(answer: str | None) -> FailureClass | None:
    78	    if not answer:
    79	        return None
    80	    a = answer.strip().lower()
    81	    for cls in FailureClass:
    82	        if a == cls.value or a == cls.value.replace("_", " "):

    84	    return _LETTERS.get(a[:1]) if len(a) == 1 else None

    88	    sig = classify_mod.signature(error_text)
    89	    known = precedents.lookup(sig)
    90	    if known is not None:
    91	        neatlogs.log("precedent reused", signature=sig, failure_class=known.value)

    99	        if cls.confidence >= STORE_CONFIDENT:

## cfo.ai Shows the Old Cap Runs Out of Cash in Month 14

Ari built the model in cfo.ai over MCP, in workspace "Atharva CFOAI", page "FirstRun model". Every formula reads its number from a "FirstRun drivers" table, and its "Driver source" column names the neatlogs trace behind each measured cost. The figures below were read back from cfo.ai, not computed by hand. Cost per run is $0.01862, the 64-trace mean plus compute. Gross margin includes Stripe fees.

| Scenario | Scale gross margin | Team gross margin | Month 18 MRR | Month 18 cash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | 77.1% | 84.3% | $2,069 | $16,685 |
| Growth | 77.1% | 84.3% | $5,427 | $44,674 |
| Tail month: every run at p95 cost | 41.9% | 62.9% | $2,069 | $12,503 |
| Old cap: every Scale run at $0.50 | -406.7% | 84.3% | $2,069 | -$12,212 |
| Scale at $529 | 85.8% | 84.3% | $2,875 | $21,146 |
| Scale at 1,500 runs | 87.0% | 84.3% | $2,069 | $17,280 |

Under the old cap, cash first goes negative in December 2027, month 14. Every other Scenario has positive net cash flow, so cfo.ai shows no runway limit. Raising Scale to $529 earns the most cash. Halving the Scale allowance keeps the $299 price and still clears the 70% floor.

## Both Scenarios Pay Back Fixed Costs in Month 2

This hand-built table came before the cfo.ai model and uses the v1 cost of $0.02771 per run. The cfo.ai table above uses the 64-trace cost, so its month 18 cash is higher.

Both scenarios start with $5,000 cash on 2026-11-01. Fixed costs are $25 a month. Monthly churn is 10% on Free, 5% on Team and 3% on Scale. Stripe takes 2.9% plus $0.30 per paid invoice.

- **Base:** 10 new Free users a month. 1 new Team customer a month in months 2 to 6, then 2 a month. 1 new Scale customer in months 9, 12, 15 and 18.
- **Growth:** 30 new Free users a month. 3 new Team customers a month. 1 new Scale customer a month from month 4.

340 341 ### cfo.ai Prices the Nightly Check 342 343 344 345 346 361 362

Ari, the cfo.ai agent, on day one.		 347 348 The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads 88 neatlogs traces and writes [business/drivers.csv](business/drivers.csv) for cfo.ai. The mean run costs $0.0178, and the p95 run costs $0.0529. A 70% margin floor turns those costs into a cap per tier, and `firstrun run --tier scale` stops any run that spends past the cap. 349 350 | Tier | Price | Quickstarts | Cap per run | Runs over the cap | 351 |---|---|---|---|---| 352 | Free | $0 | 1, weekly | $0.0135 | 50.0% | 353 | Team | $49 a month | 10, nightly | $0.0470 | 9.1% | 354 | Scale | $299 a month | 100, nightly, with PRs, Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | $0.0279 | 26.1% | 355 356 The old fixed cap of $0.50 let one bad month cost a Scale customer's fee five times over. The plan, the Scale fix and every assumption are in [business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md](business/BUSINESS_PLAN.md). The cfo.ai model is public at [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE). Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. 357 358 The [plan page](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/plan/) shows the caps, the measured cost spread and the cash per Scenario. Every doc-test run is tagged against the caps. A neatlogs alert uses the Scale cap as its threshold, and `scripts/neatlogs_issues.py` mirrors each detection and alert as a GitHub issue labeled [`neatlogs`](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/issues?q=label%3Aneatlogs). 359 360

537	## Version 2 Finishes 3 of 4 Quickstarts and Recovers 3 Failed Steps
538	
539	v1 ran with recovery off. v2 ran after the neatlogs planner fix (3ca6f11), with recovery and verification on. The same four targets ran both times. Cost and duration come from the neatlogs traces in [evidence/before_after_traces.json](evidence/before_after_traces.json). Cost is the Sonnet 5.5 list price and is not billed, because the runs use a subscription token.
540	
541	| Target | v1 (recovery off) | v2 (neatlogs fix, recovery, verify) |
542	|---|---|---|
543	| neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 | passed 3/3 |
544	| Entire CLI install | failed at step 1, `curl: command not found` | verified 4/4 after 2 fixes, one of them a real docs fix |
545	| Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 | passed 2/2 |
546	| OpenAI v0 README (fixture, Wayback 2023-08-02) | failed at step 6, `openai: command not found` | pinned `openai==0.28.1`, then stopped honestly: the example needs an OpenAI key |
547	
548	| Metric | v1 | v2 |
549	|---|---|---|
550	| Quickstarts that end passed or verified | 2 of 4 | 3 of 4 |
551	| Failed steps recovered | 0 | 3 |
552	| Fixes proven in a fresh container | 0 | 1 |
553	| Average tool spans per run | 4.25 | 6.0 |
554	| Average cost per run, from neatlogs | $0.0262 | $0.0200 |
555	| Average run time, verification included | 128 s | 201 s |
556	
557	v2 takes longer because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart a second time in a new container.
558	
559	The six mistakes the agent made in v1:
560	
561	1. The plan changes between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later.
562	2. The planner invents steps. It added `command -v entire` and `test -f first_trace.py`, which the docs never say.
563	3. The planner writes placeholder steps. Chroma step 2 is `true`.
564	4. A fake secret passes as a step. `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0.
565	5. The planner skips the steps that matter, because they need a key.
566	6. 9 of 16 steps check only the exit code.
567	
568	## What Broke While Building
569	
570	- **Git 2.33 hung Entire checkpoints.** The post-commit hook waited 206 s on `git update-ref --stdin`, and the checkpoint was never written. Git 2.55.0 fixed it, and the next hook took 3 s.
571	- **One run split into 3 traces.** The first live run on the neatlogs docs produced 3 traces. The CLI now opens one `firstrun.run` trace around reading, planning, every step and verification.
